name: Spanish spade beard

image.caption: Poland Epitaph portrait of a man with spade beard

lead: The Spanish spade beard is a sixteenth-century facial hair style in which the beard is shaped into a spade at the chin. It appears in lists of European beard styles that came back into fashion after the Reformation, alongside the English square cut, forked and stiletto beards.

The look is used to frame the jaw and lengthen the chin visually, giving a stronger, more defined lower face. No studies have examined this particular style; research on beards generally covers perceived dominance and attractiveness.

paras: Growers let the chin and cheek hair fill in, then trim the sides to a spade outline with a trimmer or razor and keep the cheeks and neck line tidy. Upkeep is regular trimming to hold the outline.
Low-risk grooming. Razor bumps and ingrown hairs along the shaved edges are possible for people prone to them.

angle.text: A shaped beard changes the silhouette of the lower face, adding length and definition at the chin. It is adjustable and reversible by trimming.

lead: The Spanish spade beard is one of several beard shapes from the sixteenth century. Wikipedia lists it with the English square cut, the forked beard and the stiletto beard as styles that emerged when beards became fashionable again after the Reformation.[1]

For people working on their look, a shaped beard can change the visual outline of the lower face. Research on facial hair in general reports that clean-shaven faces are rated as less dominant than bearded ones and that facial hairiness appears to influence male attractiveness, though scholars have not settled whether this relates to attractiveness or dominance.[1]

paras: After a period of clean-shaven fashion, beards returned in sixteenth-century Europe, producing named styles including the Spanish spade.[1] Shaving then became more common among European elites in the late 1600s, and upper and middle-class men were largely clean-shaven by the eighteenth century.[1]

Wikipedia reports findings that bearded men are rated as more dominant than clean-shaven ones and that facial hair influences perceived male attractiveness.[1] No study specific to the spade shape has been published.

timeline.event: Beards return to fashion after the Reformation, with styles including the Spanish spade.[1]
